whatItFakes: The state-chamber party-loyalty weight (weights.statePartyLoyalty, 1) is checked against the federal party-unity figure (about 0.90, CQ Vote Studies) because the state roll-call calibration input is not in the repository.
why: The owner ruled on Oct 15 that his own state roll-call input may calibrate this one parameter, with nothing from it shipped or cited; a builder session does not hold that input.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Run the owner's state roll-call input against the simulated chambers (src/core2/party-loyalty.test.ts measures them), set statePartyLoyalty and the test's target from it, and close this row.

whatItFakes: A state's grocery exemption spares groceries from every level's sales tax in the town, as if every state's local sales taxes followed the state's base. A county's or city's exemption spares only its own tax.
why: No place data says which states let local sales taxes still reach groceries the state exempts (for example home-rule cities, or local option taxes kept on food), so the engine takes the common case of a uniform base.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A per-state field in the starting-law research (data/research/laws/local-starting-law/sales-tax.json) saying whether local sales taxes follow the state's grocery exemption, sourced from each state's revenue department, read here so a state exemption spares only the levels its base covers.

whatItFakes: A lobbying ban with no numeric period on its law row retains the existing estimated two-year cooling-off period. Researched numeric periods are read from the actual law instead.
why: Some researched yes answers have no structured period, and a newly enacted yes/no bill can omit a duration. This item fixes continuous service and reads available provisions without inventing missing statutory detail.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Supply the missing structured periods through researched starting-law and voted bill provisions; remove the fallback when every applicable ban carries one.

whatItFakes: A bordering state's law on a question, which weighs on a state legislator's reason to carry the same change (neighborLawWeight), is that state's researched starting law, not its law in force: only the town's state legislates in a played world, so no other state's own acts are recorded and a neighbor never changes its law.
why: Other states keep only coarse results; their legislatures do not sit in the played world.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Read each bordering state's law in force from the laws a coarse state legislature enacts for it, so a neighbor's change reaches its neighbors the next session.

whatItFakes: Six federal questions start as law in force (each cited) and Congress can enact or repeal them from the bill paper, but no engine reads the law at the moment it decides or pays, so enacting one moves no money, person or place: student loan forgiveness, D.C. statehood and the members' stock trading ban are read by nothing at all; housing vouchers for every eligible family, limits on power plant carbon and raising tariffs move only the outcome web's ledger (housing-vouchers-to-homelessness, power-plant-carbon-to-emissions and -particulates, tariffs-to-prices), with no person, household or business recorded as reached. Read now, and so no longer here: immigration (counted-moves.ts raises the yearly arrivals from abroad and records them), federal mandatory minimums (federal-courts.ts shortens the sentences of new admissions), national data privacy (the business engine charges employing businesses a compliance cost), the disaster cost share (disasters.ts) and the debt limit (budgets-treasury.ts).
why: Each needs a mechanic or a researched size that does not exist yet (a debt ceiling that binds borrowing, an immigration flow, a loan balance record, a disaster cost split, a privacy rule that businesses follow, a statehood and representation change, a sentencing record, a members' holdings record).
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: One reader per question, each from its research (data/research/campaigns/federal-questions-2026.json names the cheapest reader for each), so enacting the law changes a record another engine reads.

whatItFakes: How big a gap between a member's wanted budget line and the line in force must be before they file a mid-year amendment (1 percent of the line, spread 0.5 to 3 percent, budgetAmendmentMinShare) is an estimate; no table of local amendment thresholds was found. Real councils also take up contracts, appointments and rezonings that no record here carries.
why: The research names how often local bodies amend budgets mid-year but not a size below which members do not bother.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: Thresholds from sampled local budget-amendment codes and agendas.

whatItFakes: The federal share of public assistance once Congress has states share disaster costs is the 50 percent FEMA's head said was coming (May 15, 2025, Reuters), spread 25 to 75 percent (disasterFederalShareWhenStatesShare); no enacted bill sets it. The cut applies to the federal public assistance the declaration pays the county and town governments.
why: Only the administration's stated plan names the replacement share; no bill or rule has set it.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The share from the first enacted or introduced text, with the state's own cost taken up by the state government's budget.

whatItFakes: Where Congress has made a higher debt limit something to pay for, the statutory limit ($41.1 trillion, P.L. 119-21, scaled to this world's debt) holds and the Treasury borrows only the room under it, its payments prorated; no offsetting cuts to pay for a raise are drawn up, and the limit is not raised by any other route. Where the law is off, the limit is raised whenever it binds (today's practice), so borrowing is unlimited.
why: The research names the limit and the votes but no schedule of offsets; the raise-and-offset bargain is not simulated.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: The federal budget's adoption cutting lines by the 'pay for' amount of each raise, from the first enacted or introduced text.

whatItFakes: A law allowing residential retail electric choice cuts every household's electricity spending by 7 percent, fading to nothing over five years from its effective date (Su 2015). The cut is the average over states, which research traces to the rate freezes and cuts legislated with restructuring; no rate freeze is drawn up, no state-by-state size is used, and the starting law in the 14 states that already have choice dates from 1998 to 2002, so it has faded to nothing there.
why: Published estimates differ by sample and method (Hill finds the cut comes from rate freezes; Borenstein and Bushnell find no significant effect after controlling for gas prices), and none is per state.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A state-by-state price effect from the restructuring acts' own rate freezes and cuts, with the supplier market (shopping share) as the competition term.

whatItFakes: A claim from a worker with fewer than five completed quarters of recorded pay (a job or a world under about a year and a quarter old) is not read from the first four of the last five completed quarters: with exactly four, the base is those four (the last completed quarter included, so an hours cut in it moves the benefit); with fewer, the weekly benefit is the state's share of the lost job's weekly pay as it stood on the last day, times the weeks it ran (capped by the weekly maximum). A worker with five or more completed quarters is read from the base period, the highest quarter, the two highest or the base year as the state's row says (proved Nov 11: an hours cut in the last completed quarter leaves the claim equal to the steady-hours twin's).
why: No per-person pay by calendar quarter is read by the claim engine; named workers' paydays are in the cash journal (work-payroll-cash.ts) and counted workers' in their group's perDayMinorByJob history, but the claim does not sum them yet.
replacement: States' alternative base period (the last four completed quarters) for a worker with fewer than five, and a worker with under four completed quarters reads the pay on record at the state's rule instead of the last day's pay.

whatItFakes: Each state's days to answer a public-records request (recordsDays, 43 of 56 places with a number, the rest ESTIMATED FROM AVERAGE by median) sit in the research file but are not loaded as law: nothing in the game files or answers a records request, so no engine could read the number.
why: The game has no records request: a resident, reporter or the player cannot ask an office for a record, and no office answers one within days. The notice hours in the same file are loaded and read (scheduleVote). Dropped by the owner, Nov 10, 2026; its research is kept.
replacement: Dropped Nov 10, 2026 (too in depth, owner): the estimate stays as the game's answer. Was: A records request a resident or the player can file with an office, answered within the state's days from the office's own staff time, with the delay and the denial kept as records; then load recordsDaysUsed as a law series and read it where the office answers.
